ai.description: This file implements core logic for building and applying transactions to ledgers in the XRPL (XRP Ledger) system. The main function, buildLedgerImpl, creates a new ledger from a parent, applies a set of transactions, updates ledger state (including NegativeUNL and skip lists), and finalizes the ledger. The applyTransactions function processes a set of transactions in multiple passes, handling retries and failures, and logs the results. There are two overloads of buildLedger: one for building a ledger from a parent and a transaction set, and another for building a ledger from replay data. The code ensures ledger consistency, handles transaction application logic, and manages ledger metadata updates, with extensive logging and error handling throughout.

This file implements the core logic for the transaction queue (TxQ) in the XRPL server. The TxQ manages transactions that cannot be immediately applied to the open ledger, handling queuing, prioritization, and eventual application or removal. Key features include: calculation of fee levels paid and required, dynamic adjustment of queue and fee escalation parameters based on ledger activity, logic for replacing or removing transactions in the queue, and mechanisms for applying queued transactions when conditions allow. The queue enforces per-account and global limits, supports transaction replacement with higher fees, and penalizes accounts for repeated failures. The file also provides metrics and RPC reporting for queue status and fee levels. Configuration is supported via a setup function that reads parameters from the server config. The main classes are TxQ (the queue itself), TxQ::FeeMetrics (for fee escalation and queue sizing), TxQ::MaybeTx (a queued transaction), and TxQ::TxQAccount (per-account transaction management).

This file implements the core network operations logic for the XRPL server (rippled). The main class, NetworkOPsImp, manages the server's operating mode, transaction processing (both synchronous and asynchronous), consensus participation, ledger publication, and subscription management for various real-time data streams (such as ledgers, transactions, validations, and account history). It handles state transitions (disconnected, connected, syncing, tracking, full), processes incoming and outgoing transactions, manages transaction batches, and coordinates consensus rounds. The class also provides mechanisms for clients to subscribe/unsubscribe to server events and account-specific updates, including historical transaction streaming. It tracks server fee metrics, publishes server and consensus status, and manages resource usage. The implementation includes detailed state accounting for monitoring and reporting, and supports both standalone and networked operation modes. The file also contains logic for handling book offers, peer status, and validator list management, ensuring the server stays in sync with the network and provides up-to-date information to clients.

This file implements the core logic for the 'simulate' RPC handler in the XRPL server. It allows clients to simulate the application of a transaction to the current open ledger without actually submitting it. The main function, doSimulate, processes incoming parameters, validates and parses the transaction (from either JSON or binary blob), autofills missing fields (like Fee, Sequence, SigningPubKey, etc.), and ensures the transaction is unsigned. It then constructs a Transaction object and applies it in 'dry run' mode using the transaction queue, returning the simulated result, including engine result codes, messages, and optional metadata in either JSON or binary format. The code includes robust error handling for malformed input, missing fields, and unsupported transaction types (like batch transactions). The file is structured around several helper functions for autofilling transaction fields, extracting transaction JSON from parameters, and formatting the simulation result.

The file defines helper functions for evaluating transaction consequences, calculating base fees, and invoking the main transaction lifecycle steps: preflight (initial validation), preclaim (further checks before application), and apply (executing the transaction). It handles unknown transaction types with a custom exception and logs errors appropriately. The file also defines the TxConsequences class, which encapsulates the effects and costs of a transaction. Overall, this file is central to the transaction processing pipeline, ensuring that each transaction type is handled according to its specific logic and that errors are managed robustly.

Each invariant checker provides visitEntry and finalize methods to inspect ledger changes and validate invariants after transaction execution. The file also defines a tuple type, InvariantChecks, aggregating all these checkers, and a function to instantiate them. These invariants help ensure ledger integrity and prevent protocol violations during transaction processing.

The class also handles transaction application, including updating account state, consuming sequence numbers or tickets, and managing transaction metadata. The Transactor class provides methods for transaction sequence checking, fee calculation, signature verification (single and multi-sign), permission checks, and ticket deletion. The file is central to the transaction lifecycle, ensuring that all necessary checks and state updates are performed before a transaction is applied to the ledger.

This file implements core logic for applying and validating transactions in the XRPL (XRP Ledger) server. It defines several functions to check transaction validity, force validity flags, and apply transactions (including batch transactions) to the ledger. The checkValidity function uses a HashRouter to cache and check signature and local validity results, handling both regular and batch transactions. The apply functions orchestrate the preflight checks and actual application of transactions, supporting both single and batched transactions. The applyBatchTransactions function processes each transaction in a batch according to batch mode flags (all-or-nothing, until-failure, only-one). The applyTransaction function is the main entry point for applying a transaction, handling retries, logging, and invoking batch processing if needed. The code ensures that transactions are only applied if they pass signature and local checks, and manages the application of batch transactions atomically or partially based on flags. Exception handling and detailed logging are included for robustness and traceability.

The class supports single and multi-signature transactions, with methods for signing, signature verification, and extracting transaction details such as type, sequence, mentioned accounts, and transaction ID. It also includes methods for JSON serialization, SQL metadata generation, and batch transaction handling. The file defines transaction SQL status enums, and provides utility functions for local checks, transaction sterilization, and pseudo-transaction identification. The design enforces canonical signatures and supports protocol rule checks for expanded signer lists.

ai.description: This file defines the OpenLedger class, which manages the current open ledger in the XRPL (XRP Ledger) server. It provides thread-safe access and modification to the open ledger, allowing transactions to be applied, retried, or rejected according to specific rules and flags. The class uses mutexes for concurrency control and maintains a shared pointer to the current OpenView. Key methods include checking if the ledger is empty, accessing the current view, modifying the ledger with a user-provided function, and accepting new transactions with retry logic. The file also includes utility functions for debugging transaction and ledger states. The OpenLedger class is non-copyable and must be constructed with a ledger, cache, and logging journal. The apply method implements the logic for applying transactions, handling retries, and ensuring consistency. The file is part of the core ledger management infrastructure in the XRPL server.

This file defines the Transaction class and related types for handling transactions in the Ripple (XRPL) server. The Transaction class encapsulates a transaction's data, status, result, and provides methods for managing its lifecycle, including construction from SQL, status management, result setting, and JSON serialization. It tracks transaction state (such as whether it is new, included, conflicted, etc.), supports marking as applying, and manages submission results (applied, broadcast, queued, kept). The class also stores and provides access to current ledger state relevant to the transaction. Static methods allow loading and locating transactions by ID, including searching within ledger ranges. Supporting structures include enums for transaction status, a struct for submission results, a struct for current ledger state, and a locator for transaction search results. The file includes necessary dependencies and forward declarations for integration with the broader application.

It provides mechanisms to insert ledgers into caches, retrieve them by hash or sequence number, and handle mismatches between built and validated ledgers. The class maintains two main caches: one for ledgers by hash and another for consensus-validated ledgers by index. It includes detailed logging and comparison functions to analyze and report differences between ledgers, especially in cases of mismatches during consensus. The file also provides utility functions for cache maintenance, such as clearing old entries and fixing index-to-hash mappings. Overall, LedgerHistory is central to ensuring ledger consistency and diagnosing consensus issues in the XRPL server.

It handles state transitions (disconnected, connected, syncing, tracking, full), processes incoming and outgoing transactions, manages transaction batches, and coordinates consensus rounds. It tracks server fee metrics, publishes server and consensus status, and manages resource usage. The file also contains logic for handling book offers, peer status, and validator list management, ensuring the server stays in sync with the network and provides up-to-date information to clients.
